A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same InterRVOS/ReVIOSa research. All 31 pages of v1 and 30 pages of v3, including appendices, figures, tables and equations, support comparison. Renamed datasets and relocated material can be matched.

before.justification: v1 reports original segmentation experiments, architectural ablations, training-dataset comparisons and zero-shot results in Tables 3–6 and A1–A2.

after.justification: v3 reports original actor/target segmentation results, attention-loss ablations, attention analyses and benchmark evaluations in Tables 2–4, Tables A1–A3 and Appendix B.

M1.justification: v1 already uses separate actor/target tokens with InternVL and SAM2. v3 adds attention mask loss: selected segmentation-token attention maps receive binary cross-entropy supervision against resized object masks. Selecting the strongest vision-attending layer and its top-four heads introduces a substantive new training component, beyond expanded documentation of the existing architecture.

E1.justification: Both versions cover interaction-aware and standard RVOS using the VidOR-derived dataset, MeViS, Ref-Youtube-VOS and Ref-DAVIS, with MeViS, ReVOS and Ref-SAV training comparisons. InterRVOS-8K/2K/5K become InterRVOS-127K/28K/71K through expression-count naming. Revised sample counts and additional evaluations remain within the existing data and task coverage.

E2.justification: v3 Table 2 adds VISA-7B and VideoLISA-3.8B to the main comparison while retaining Referformer, LMPM and Sa2VA-1B/4B from v1 Table 5. The new standard-benchmark comparison in v3 Table A1 includes LISA, TrackGPT and VISA at multiple model sizes, substantially broadening the reported comparator set.

E3.justification: v1 Table 5 separates Referring, Actor-Target and Overall samples; v3 Table 2 separately scores actor and target outputs on interaction expressions and reports RVOS over all expressions. The evaluation set remains 738 videos but changes from 5,126 to 5,048 expressions. Zero-shot comparisons switch from InterRVOS-5K to the full training dataset, and v3 adds standard-benchmark evaluation of an AML-only variant.

E4.justification: v3 adds component ablations for tokens and AML, layer/head sensitivity tests, attention–segmentation correlation analysis, actor/target attention comparisons and supervised versus unsupervised head visualizations. These substantially expand mechanism analysis. Conversely, v1's independent-versus-joint token comparison and caption-type breakdowns on InterRVOS and MeViS are removed (v1 Tables 4, 6 and A1).

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or statistical significance tests. The new attention averages describe model behavior rather than uncertainty across experimental runs.

E6.justification: The main results are revised: v1 Table 5 reports overall J&F of 59.7/60.0 for ReVIOSa-1B/4B; v3 Table 2 reports RVOS scores of 62.0/64.5 and newly separate target scores of 67.4/68.3. Changed evaluation settings prevent treating these as controlled cross-version gains. v3 also adds AML and standard-benchmark results and replaces zero-shot results under changed training-set size. The MeViS dataset comparison remains numerically unchanged between v1 Table 3 and v3 Table A2.

T1.justification: v3 introduces the mathematical definition of AML and its incorporation into the total objective (Equations 6 and 8). This is a limited substantive mathematical addition. Much of the other new notation formalizes previously described prompting and mask prediction; neither version supplies theoretical guarantees or proofs.

C1.justification: v3 adds AML as a central methodological contribution in the abstract, introduction and conclusion, claiming improved role-specific grounding. It also foregrounds asymmetric roles and their separate evaluation from a single expression, replacing v1's emphasis on complementary expression pairs. Single-expression dual-output segmentation itself was already claimed in v1.

C2.justification: v3 substantially expands the mechanism account: attention alignment motivates AML, similar actor/target attention supports shared layer selection, and supervision is interpreted as benefiting unsupervised heads. Appendix C.1 newly qualifies standard-benchmark applicability by using an AML-only variant. Meanwhile, v1 Appendix G's limitations concerning interaction-rich source availability and blurred or corrupted imagery disappear.

D1.justification: v3 newly documents SAM2 mask-track precomputation, human correction of evaluation expressions and masks, and exact AML layer/head selections. Reported training times change from 4/10 to 12/16 hours for 1B/4B, with epochs, batch size and hardware retained. It omits v1's explicit video-disjointness and evaluation-filtering statements; this is lost documentation, not evidence that the split became overlapping. Annotation prompts and the project-page address remain.

R1.justification: v3 adds references including LISA, TrackGPT and GLAMM and explicitly distinguishes InterRVOS from grounded conversation generation, arguing that noun-phrase grounding does not capture directional actor/target semantics. This refines the existing RVOS and interaction-reasoning positioning without replacing it.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work and architecture exposition are extensively rewritten. Dataset construction details and training-dataset comparisons move into reorganized appendices, while AML becomes a major narrative focus. Dataset terminology changes to expression-count names, and the title and author list are revised.

P2.justification: v3 adopts a two-column layout, redraws the teaser and architecture diagrams, restructures the main results table around separate actor/target outputs, and adds numerous attention plots and visualizations. Caption-type tables are removed and qualitative panels replaced. Retained dataset examples, statistics and annotation prompts are relocated or reformatted rather than newly introduced.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially improves validation of the central actor/target distinction: Table 2 reports each output role separately, addressing v1 Table 5's lack of separate role measurements. Component and layer/head ablations also provide concrete support for the new AML design, alongside broader baseline comparisons. Removing caption-type analyses, explicit limitations and split-disjointness documentation weakens transparency, but the stronger task-specific evaluation and methodological evidence provide a substantial net improvement.
